Utilities & C Compatibility

On this page

SIMD (std::simd) ​

std/simd/ is a portable SIMD library built entirely on vec<T, N>, the compiler's native vector type — there is no hand-written per-instruction implementation anywhere in this library. Elementwise arithmetic and lane access already work on any vec<T,N> through ordinary operator/subscript syntax; this library adds convenient ISA-agnostic type names, pointer load/store, broadcast, horizontal reductions, and fused multiply-add on top.

c
#include <std/simd/simd.h>

int main() {
    float src[4] = {1.0, 5.0, 3.0, 2.0};
    float dst[4];

    f32x4 v = std::simd_load_f32x4(&src[0]);
    f32x4 doubled = v + v;
    std::simd_store_f32x4(doubled, &dst[0]);

    float total = std::simd_hsum_f32x4(v);      // horizontal sum
    f32x4 a = std::simd_splat_f32x4(2.0);       // broadcast
    f32x4 fma = std::simd_fma_f32x4(a, a, v);   // a*a + v
    return 0;
}

Load and store take a reference to the first element and read or write N consecutive elements from there, as one unaligned vector load or store. Passing the address of an array element (&src[0]) needs no unsafe.

Type Aliases ​

Naming convention: <elem><bits>x<lanes>. Widths cover every target's baseline SIMD register (128-bit: SSE, NEON, WASM SIMD128, RVV with VLEN≥128) plus the common 256-bit case (AVX2 — on targets without a native 256-bit register, LLVM legalizes it into two 128-bit ops, still correct, just not a single instruction).

AliasUnderlying type
f32x4, f32x8vec<float, 4>, vec<float, 8>
f64x2, f64x4vec<double, 2>, vec<double, 4>
i32x4, i32x8vec<int, 4>, vec<int, 8>
i64x2, i64x4vec<long long, 2>, vec<long long, 4>
i16x8, i16x16vec<short, 8>, vec<short, 16>
i8x16, i8x32vec<signed char, 16>, vec<signed char, 32>
u32x4, u32x8vec<unsigned int, 4>, vec<unsigned int, 8>
u8x16, u8x32vec<unsigned char, 16>, vec<unsigned char, 32>

Functions ​

FunctionDescription
simd_load_<type>(const &T p)Load N lanes starting at p — unaligned by construction
simd_store_<type>(v, &T p)Store N lanes starting at p
simd_splat_<type>(x)Broadcast a scalar to every lane
simd_fma_<type>(a, b, c)Multiply-add a*b + c, as one fused instruction where the target has FMA
simd_min_<type>(a, b) / simd_max_<type>(a, b)Elementwise min/max
simd_hsum_<type>(v)Horizontal sum — reduce all lanes to one scalar
simd_hmin_<type>(v) / simd_hmax_<type>(v)Horizontal min/max

Not every function is defined for every type alias. The exact set:

FunctionTypes
simd_load_* / simd_store_*f32x4, f32x8, f64x2, f64x4, i32x4, i32x8, u32x4, u32x8, i8x16, u8x16
simd_splat_*f32x4, f32x8, f64x2, f64x4, i32x4, i32x8, u32x4
simd_fma_*f32x4, f32x8, f64x2, f64x4
simd_min_* / simd_max_*f32x4, f32x8, i32x4
simd_hsum_*f32x4, f32x8, f64x2, f64x4, i32x4, i32x8, u32x4
simd_hmin_* / simd_hmax_*f32x4

For anything else, use the native vec<T, N> operators directly (see Native SIMD).

c
#include <std/simd/simd.h>

float dot4(const &float a, const &float b) {
    f32x4 va = std::simd_load_f32x4(a);
    f32x4 vb = std::simd_load_f32x4(b);
    f32x4 acc = std::simd_fma_f32x4(va, vb, std::simd_splat_f32x4(0.0f));
    return std::simd_hsum_f32x4(acc);
}

CPU SIMD levels — cpu.h ​

c
#include <std/simd/cpu.h>

std's hot kernels — sgemm, vmath.h, the FFT butterflies and dsp_dot_f64 — are built in several versions and use the best one the CPU supports, in this order:

FamilyOrderChosen
x86-64AVX-512 (F+BW+DQ+VL) > AVX2 + FMA > AVX > SSE4.1 > SSE2at run time (cpuid + xgetbv), once
AArch64SVE > Neonat run time on Linux (getauxval), else Neon
Cortex-MHelium (MVE) > DSP extensionat compile time, by target: arm-81m for Helium, arm-7em / arm-8m for DSP
WebAssemblySIMD128at compile time

So one x86-64 binary built for the portable baseline uses AVX-512 where the CPU has it and still runs on an SSE2-only machine. Whatever the build already guarantees (for instance --target-cpu=native, which defines __AVX2__ etc.; see ISA macros) is the floor. Each version is the same source compiled with __attribute__((target(...))).

c
#define SIMD_SSE2 1   // ... SIMD_SSE41 2, SIMD_AVX 3, SIMD_AVX2 4, SIMD_AVX512 5,
                      // SIMD_NEON 10, SIMD_SVE 11, SIMD_DSP 20, SIMD_HELIUM 21, SIMD_WASM128 30
int simd_level();                     // detected once, then cached
const &char simd_level_name(int level);   // "AVX-512", "Neon", "Helium", ...

SAFEC_SIMD=sse2|sse4.1|avx|avx2|avx512|neon|sve caps the level, to test or compare the slower paths.

Matrix multiply — gemm.h ​

c
#include <std/simd/gemm.h>

Single-precision GEMM for the CPU. A and B are packed into contiguous strips and multiplied by a register-tile kernel: 4 × 16 on vec<float, 8> (SSE2, AVX, AVX2 + FMA builds of one body) or 8 × 16 on vec<float, 16> for AVX-512. C is cut into tiles that run on the thread pool once a product has about a million multiply-adds.

When the program links a CPU vendor BLAS, its kernels do the work: AOCL-BLAS on AMD, oneMKL on Intel, Accelerate on Apple. safeguard's [build] blas links the right one; by hand, link -lblis-mt -lgomp, oneMKL's mkl_intel_lp64 mkl_gnu_thread mkl_core -lgomp, or -framework Accelerate. sgemm reaches cblas_sgemm through a weak reference, so the choice is made at link time. Except with Accelerate, std runs the library on one thread and splits C across its own pool, one library call per tile. The libraries' OpenMP workers busy-wait between calls, and on the same cores as the pool that made a U-Net forward pass six times slower. This setting also makes the library single-threaded for the program's own direct calls into it.

c
#define SGEMM_NO_TRANS 0
#define SGEMM_TRANS    1

// C = alpha * op(A) * op(B) + beta * C, row-major; op(A) is m x k, op(B) is k x n.
// 'ld' = elements between the starts of two rows. beta == 0 never reads C.
void sgemm(int transA, int transB, unsigned long m, unsigned long n, unsigned long k,
           float alpha, const &float a, unsigned long lda,
           const &float b, unsigned long ldb,
           float beta, &float c, unsigned long ldc);

// Same, always on the calling thread (no pool; a vendor library, if linked,
// runs single-threaded): for code that is already parallel.
void sgemm_serial(/* same parameters */);

int sgemm_vendor();            // 1 if a vendor BLAS is in use
const &char sgemm_backend();   // "AOCL-BLAS (BLIS)", "oneMKL", "Accelerate", "OpenBLAS", "CBLAS", "built-in"

tensor_matmul (forward and backward, for every element type) and Conv2D::forward are built on it.

Throughput on a Ryzen 7 7800X3D (Zen 4, 8 cores / 16 threads), N × N × N, from one baseline x86-64 build:

Kernel1 thread, N = 102416 threads, N = 51216 threads, N = 1024
built-in, SSE2 (SAFEC_SIMD=sse2)35 GFLOP/s252 GFLOP/s239 GFLOP/s
built-in, AVX86 GFLOP/s575 GFLOP/s614 GFLOP/s
built-in, AVX2 + FMA100 GFLOP/s575 GFLOP/s614 GFLOP/s
built-in, AVX-512 (picked on this CPU)105 GFLOP/s671 GFLOP/s716 GFLOP/s
AOCL-BLAS 5.3, tiles on std's pool134 GFLOP/s1007 GFLOP/s1074 GFLOP/s
oneMKL 2026.2, tiles on std's pool130 GFLOP/s671 GFLOP/s716 GFLOP/s

Vector math — vmath.h ​

c
#include <std/simd/vmath.h>
void vm_exp_f32(const &float x, &float y, unsigned long n);
void vm_tanh_f32(const &float x, &float y, unsigned long n);
void vm_sigmoid_f32(const &float x, &float y, unsigned long n);

y[i] = f(x[i]) as branch-free polynomial code (Cephes-style range reduction), vectorized at the CPU's SIMD level and split across the thread pool from 32,768 elements. Measured error is under 1 ulp for exp, 1.3 ulp for tanh and 2 ulp for sigmoid, subnormal results included. NaN propagates and overflow gives infinity. About 0.2 ns per element on the 7800X3D. x and y may be the same array. std's activations (sigmoid, tanh, GELU, SiLU, ELU, GLU, SwiGLU) and softmax use it.

Per-ISA Convenience Headers ​

Eight thin headers re-export the same portable types under architecture-idiomatic names — each is pure typedefs and documentation, containing no separate logic, and each has been verified against real generated code for its target (disassembled llc output, not just "compiles"):

HeaderTargetNative mapping
std/simd/x86_64.hx86_64m128/m128i/m128d (SSE/SSE2), m256/m256i/m256d (AVX/AVX2)
std/simd/aarch64.hAArch64128-bit NEON registers
std/simd/riscv.hRISC-V (+v)128-bit RVV register groups (baseline zve* width; a true scalable vector length isn't modeled — see the header for why)
std/simd/wasm.hWebAssembly128-bit v128 (SIMD128 proposal)
std/simd/spirv.hSPIR-VReal OpTypeVector/OpFAdd in a compute kernel body — see the header's caveat about SPIR-V's no-host-libc execution model
std/simd/cortex_m.hARM Cortex-MMVE (M55/M85) type aliases + the DSP-extension dsp_* functions (M4/M7) — see Bare-Metal
std/simd/cuda.hCUDA (NVPTX)Real PTX vector-lane codegen — GPU scalarizes to N scalar ops, see caveat below
std/simd/rocm.hROCm (AMDGPU)Real GCN vector-ALU codegen — same scalarization caveat

Cortex-M DSP intrinsics ​

On Cortex-M4/M7 (+dsp) the packed-SIMD instructions work on 2×16-bit or 4×8-bit lanes inside one 32-bit register, and LLVM does not vectorize vec<T, N> into them. std/simd/cortex_m.h therefore exposes them as functions, each compiling to the single named instruction:

FunctionInstruction
dsp_qadd(a, b) / dsp_qsub(a, b)saturating 32-bit add / subtract
dsp_qadd16, dsp_qsub16, dsp_qadd8, dsp_qsub8saturating signed add / subtract per 16-bit or 8-bit lane
dsp_uqadd16, dsp_uqsub16, dsp_uqadd8, dsp_uqsub8saturating unsigned, per lane
dsp_sadd16, dsp_ssub16, dsp_sadd8, dsp_ssub8wrapping signed, per lane
dsp_smlad(a, b, acc) / dsp_smladxdual 16×16 multiply, add both products to acc (x: halves of b swapped)
dsp_smlsd(a, b, acc) / dsp_smlsdxdual multiply, add the difference of the products to acc
dsp_smuad(a, b) / dsp_smuadxdual multiply, sum of products
dsp_smusd(a, b) / dsp_smusdxdual multiply, difference of products
dsp_usad8(a, b) / dsp_usada8(a, b, acc)sum of absolute differences of four bytes (plus acc)
dsp_sxtab16(a, b) / dsp_uxtab16(a, b)sign / zero-extend two bytes of b to 16 bits and add to a's halves

Signed variants take and return int; uq*, usad8, usada8 and uxtab16 use unsigned int. On Cortex-M55/M85 (+mve), mve_f32x4, mve_i32x4, mve_i16x8 and mve_i8x16 are native 128-bit vectors. Cortex-M0/M0+/M3/M23 have neither; vec<T, N> still works there but is scalarized.

GPU targets: SIMT, not SIMD-in-one-instruction ​

PTX and GCN have no packed-arithmetic instruction the way SSE/NEON do — a GPU's parallelism comes from running many threads in lockstep, not wide registers within one thread. vec<float,4> + vec<float,4> still compiles correctly on CUDA/ROCm targets, it just becomes four independent scalar ops rather than one wide instruction (confirmed: real generated PTX shows four add.rn.f32 instructions, real GCN shows four v_add_f32_e32 instructions). std::simd's CUDA/ROCm headers only provide the portable arithmetic types usable within a kernel body (device memory, no host libc) — they don't define kernel entry points (__global__/ ptx_kernel/amdgpu_kernel calling convention plus launch-configuration support is a separate concern this library doesn't address).

Metal Shading Language ​

Not supported. Apple's Metal compiler has no LLVM backend upstream — unlike NVPTX/AMDGPU/SPIR-V, which are real LLVM targets --target can select, Metal is a separate, closed toolchain. The only interop path from this library's SPIR-V output is a third-party translator (e.g. SPIRV-Cross), not something safec or std::simd does directly.
